title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 07–08
description: Curated B2 vocabulary for physical appearance, body shape, personality, social attitudes, register and contrasting connotations.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Study text, photographic descriptors, suffix notes, connotation table, exercises and the corresponding answer-key entries checked for lexical and usage coverage.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is given only for confident words or short phrases; longer compounds and uncertain pronunciations omit IPA. Regional variants are not exhaustively represented.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Source-page and exercise-key comparison; written editorial review of original example sentences and definitions; structural, ID, provenance and conservative audio-target checks. No live VocabLab browser import or TTS test was performed.
audit.limitations: No bundled audio files; word and example playback depend on VocabLab/browser TTS. No direct browser or speech-recognition tests were performed.

units.title: Unit 07 — Describing people: appearance
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 20–21 (PDF pages 21–22).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe hair texture, facial shape, hair colour and complexion precisely.
Choose respectful words for height and build, and distinguish slim, skinny, stocky and muscular.
Compare smart, elegant, well-dressed, scruffy, good-looking and stunning.
Use -ish for approximation in age, height and colour, and recognise descriptive opposites.
Understand exercise vocabulary for facial features, make-up and appearance.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: Her straight hair reaches just below her shoulders.
items.note: Straight hair has little or no curl; contrast wavy and curly hair.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: His wavy hair looks especially thick after it dries.
items.note: Wavy hair forms gentle waves rather than tight curls.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: She usually ties her curly hair back at work.
items.note: Hair with curls; not the same as merely wavy hair.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: He has had long hair since university.
items.note: Hair is usually uncountable when referring to all the hair on someone's head.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: The thin-faced man in the photograph is my uncle.
items.note: Describes a relatively narrow face; different from thin as a body-build description.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: A round-faced teenager answered the door.
items.note: Compound adjective describing the shape of someone's face.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: She has a thin face and striking cheekbones.
items.note: Noun phrase corresponding to thin-faced; use has a thin face, not is thin face.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: He has a round face and a friendly expression.
items.note: Noun phrase corresponding to round-faced; use has a round face.

items.pt: cabelo cortado bem curto; corte militar
items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: After the summer, he decided to get a crew-cut.
items.note: A very short hairstyle, usually clipped close to the head.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: My father went bald in his early thirties.
items.note: Adjective: be bald or go bald; do not say have bald hair.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: She has freckles across her cheeks and nose.
items.note: Small brown spots on the skin; usually used in the plural.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: He grew a beard during his holiday.
items.note: Hair growing on the lower part of a person's face.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: His grandfather has a neat grey moustache.
items.note: British spelling and pronunciation; American English typically spells mustache.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: The baby has a chubby face and bright eyes.
items.note: Chubby suggests gently rounded or plump; often used of faces, cheeks and young children.

items.pt: cabelo com entradas; cabelo rareando na frente
items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: His receding hair is more noticeable in old photographs.
items.note: A receding hairline moves back from the forehead as hair is lost.

items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: Fine wrinkles appeared around his eyes over time.
items.note: Lines in the skin, often associated with age or facial expressions.

items.pt: ficar grisalho; ficar com cabelos brancos
items.section: A · Hair texture and facial shape
items.example: Some people start to go grey in their twenties.
items.note: In British English, grey; in American English, gray.

items.example: She has blonde hair, but her eyebrows are darker.
items.note: Common for light yellowish hair; blond is also used, especially in American spelling.

items.example: A fair-haired child was waiting near the entrance.
items.note: Light-coloured hair; fair can also describe skin or complexion.

items.example: The dark-haired woman near the window is our tutor.
items.note: Hair that is brown or black; distinct from dark skin.

items.example: His ginger-haired brother has the same green eyes.
items.note: Ginger is an informal British English colour term for reddish hair.

items.example: The red-haired actor was easy to recognise.
items.note: Natural reddish hair; sometimes preferred over ginger-haired.

items.example: Her auburn hair looks almost copper-coloured in sunlight.
items.note: Reddish-brown, generally darker than bright ginger or red hair.

items.example: He has fair skin and wears sunscreen outdoors.
items.note: Fair describes relatively light skin colour; also used of hair and complexion.

items.example: The photographer adjusted the lighting for different shades of dark skin.
items.note: Dark describes skin shade; it does not by itself identify nationality or ethnicity.

items.pt: tez; aparência e tonalidade da pele do rosto
items.example: After her holiday, she had a healthy-looking complexion.
items.note: Describes the appearance and colour of facial skin, not the shape of the face.

items.example: Cold weather can leave your skin feeling dry.
items.note: Uncountable when referring generally to the covering of the body.

items.example: He tends to get a tan quickly in summer.
items.note: A tan is darker skin produced by exposure to sunlight; protect skin from harmful UV exposure.

items.pt: queimado de sol; com queimadura solar
items.example: Her shoulders were sunburnt after the walk.
items.note: British spelling sunburnt; sunburned is also common. Refers to skin damage from sun exposure.

items.example: Her older sister is unusually tall for her age.
items.note: Height, not body weight; compare short.

items.example: He is quite short, but he has a powerful build.
items.note: Describes a person's height; can also mean brief for time.

items.example: The article used the word fat when discussing body-size discrimination.
items.note: Can be direct or offensive when used about a person, depending on context and preference.

items.example: The portrait shows a plump man with a gentle smile.
items.note: Softer than fat in some contexts, but still a personal comment about body size.

items.example: He was a stout, broad-shouldered man.
items.note: Means solidly or heavily built; can sound dated when used of people.

items.example: The doctor discussed the term overweight and its limitations.
items.note: Often used in health contexts; avoid assuming health or fitness from appearance alone.

items.example: The stocky goalkeeper moved surprisingly quickly.
items.note: Short-to-medium height with a broad, solid build; not simply obese.

items.example: The well-built athlete carried the equipment easily.
items.note: Describes a strong, solid physique; often a positive term.

items.example: She has become more muscular since taking up climbing.
items.note: Describes well-developed muscles; can apply to any gender.

items.example: Obese is a medical category, not a polite everyday description of a stranger.
items.note: Clinical term about body weight; avoid using as a casual judgement from looks.

items.example: The photograph shows a tall, thin man in his fifties.
items.note: Neutral or context-dependent; compare slim and skinny.

items.example: The jacket has a slim cut that suits her figure.
items.note: Often favourable when describing a person's build; may also describe a narrow shape.

items.example: He disliked being called skinny at school.
items.note: Often negative or informal; may be hurtful when describing someone.

items.pt: corpo de proporções atraentes; silhueta bonita
items.example: The stylist said the dress gave her a nice figure.
items.note: Traditionally a compliment about body shape; nice figure is subjective and can feel intrusive.

items.example: The coach described him as having a compact build.
items.note: Noun for overall body shape and physical construction.

items.example: Everyone looked smart at the opening ceremony.
items.note: In British English, smart can mean neatly and stylishly dressed, not just intelligent.

items.example: He wore an elegant dark suit to the event.
items.note: Suggests tasteful, graceful style rather than merely tidy clothing.

items.example: She is always well-dressed, even at informal meetings.
items.note: Describes people whose clothes are stylish or suitable.

items.example: His scruffy coat made him look unprepared for the interview.
items.note: Informal negative term for untidy or shabby appearance.

items.example: An untidy-looking passenger entered the waiting room.
items.note: Means appearing untidy; in natural usage, often simply say looked untidy.

items.example: The costume was intentionally messy-looking.
items.note: More informal alternative to untidy-looking; can describe a person or an object.

items.example: She looked stunning in the green evening dress.
items.note: Very attractive or visually impressive, stronger than good-looking.

items.example: Everyone agreed that the actor was good-looking.
items.note: A general adjective for attractive appearance, often applied to all genders.

items.example: The interviewer avoided calling anyone unattractive.
items.note: Opposite of attractive; can sound harsh when applied to people.

items.example: She wore a beautiful handmade necklace.
items.note: More general than handsome; can describe people, objects and experiences.

items.example: Her grandfather was a handsome young man.
items.note: Traditionally used especially for attractive men, but also used in other contexts.

items.example: He has an attractive smile and a warm manner.
items.note: Describes appearance or qualities that appeal to people.

items.pt: traço mais bonito; característica mais atraente
items.example: She thinks her smile is her best feature.
items.note: Feature can mean a part of the face, such as the eyes or mouth.

items.example: For the role, the director valued personality over appearance.
items.note: A person's characteristic ways of thinking and behaving.

items.example: Her calm confidence made a good first impression.
items.note: Your initial judgement or reaction when meeting someone.

items.example: The new manager is tallish and wears glasses.
items.note: The suffix -ish softens or approximates a description.

items.example: The fabric is brownish rather than dark grey.
items.note: The suffix -ish means somewhat or approximately a colour.

items.example: The person at reception looked thirtyish.
items.note: Informal approximation of age; not an exact number.

items.example: The researcher is in her thirties and leads the team.
items.note: In one's thirties means between thirty and thirty-nine years old.

items.example: His eyes looked sparkly with excitement.
items.note: Sparkly eyes appear lively and bright; also describes glittering objects.

items.pt: um toque de vermelho; um leve tom avermelhado
items.example: Her dark hair has a tinge of red in the sunlight.
items.note: A tinge of a colour means a slight amount of that shade.

items.example: She prefers not to wear make-up at work.
items.note: Noun for cosmetics applied to the face; distinguish the phrasal verb make up.

items.pt: vestir-se de maneira mais elegante; arrumar-se
items.example: We decided to dress up for the celebration.
items.note: Dress up can mean wearing smarter clothes, or dressing in costume.

items.pt: de aparência comum; sem grande atrativo
items.example: The story describes the character as plain rather than glamorous.
items.note: Can describe an ordinary appearance without implying ugliness; may still sound unkind.

items.example: The suspect was described as ordinary-looking.
items.note: Neutral description: not especially distinctive or noticeable.

items.example: Her supervisor is in her twenties.
items.note: In one's twenties is the age range 20–29; contrasted with in her thirties.

sectionsChecked: A: Hair, face, skin and complexion (illustrations and text)

units.title: Unit 08 — Describing people: personality
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 22–23 (PDF pages 23–24).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish positive, informal and potentially offensive words for intellectual ability.
Describe optimism, extroversion, emotional reactions and practical judgement.
Express social behaviour using precise terms for politeness, honesty, trust and jealousy.
Identify differences in connotation between positive traits and negative interpretations.
Use natural register and avoid confusing sensible with sensitive or assertive with aggressive.

items.example: She is an intelligent analyst who asks excellent questions.
items.note: Broad term for mental ability; less informal than brainy.

items.example: The bright student quickly spotted the pattern.
items.note: Positive, often about people who learn or understand things quickly; also means full of light.

items.example: He found a clever way to solve the scheduling problem.
items.note: Can praise intelligence or ingenious solutions; contrast cunning for deceitful cleverness.

items.example: Despite his age, he is still mentally sharp.
items.note: Quick to notice and understand details; also means pointed or keen.

items.example: The investor made a shrewd assessment of the risks.
items.note: Good practical judgement, often about business or people.

items.example: She is an able engineer with years of experience.
items.note: Capable or skilful; able to do something is a grammatical pattern.

items.example: The programme supports gifted young musicians.
items.note: Having unusual natural ability, often in an academic or creative field.

items.example: A talented designer joined the studio.
items.note: Possessing a particular ability; near synonym of gifted, often with less emphasis on innate ability.

items.example: Her brainy cousin enjoys complicated puzzles.
items.note: Informal adjective for a very intelligent person; can sound teasing.

items.example: Calling a colleague stupid is both unhelpful and offensive.
items.note: Strongly negative; avoid labelling a person's ability this way.

items.example: It would be foolish to ignore the safety instructions.
items.note: Often criticises an action or decision rather than overall intelligence.

items.example: She objected when someone described her neighbour as simple.
items.note: When used about people and intelligence, can be patronising or offensive; often means uncomplicated elsewhere.

items.example: We laughed at our silly mistake.
items.note: Often milder than stupid, especially for behaviour, but context matters.

items.example: The manager apologised for calling the decision brainless.
items.note: Informal, insulting term for extremely foolish behaviour or people.

items.example: Don't be daft; the problem has a simple solution.
items.note: Informal, especially British, for silly or foolish; tone can be playful or insulting.

items.example: He criticised the idea without calling anyone dumb.
items.note: Informal and often insulting when used about intelligence; historically has also referred to inability to speak.

items.example: It is unfair to assume someone is dim because they are quiet.
items.note: Informal and potentially insulting when describing someone's ability.

items.example: The joke depended on the unfair stereotype that he was thick.
items.note: British informal and offensive when it means not intelligent; otherwise often means not thin.

items.example: The cunning thief changed his story several times.
items.note: Intelligence used to achieve aims by trickery; not always positive.

items.example: She noticed the crafty attempt to avoid responsibility.
items.note: Similar to cunning; can be mildly admiring or disapproving.

items.example: He gave a sly smile when the plan succeeded.
items.note: Suggests secretive or deceptive cleverness.

items.example: She is pessimistic about the chances of reaching an agreement.
items.note: Expecting poor outcomes; opposite of optimistic.

items.example: Despite the delay, the team remains optimistic.
items.note: Expecting favourable outcomes; contrast pessimistic.

items.example: Try to look on the bright side of the unexpected change.
items.note: Idiom for focusing on positive aspects of a difficult situation.

items.example: She is extroverted and enjoys meeting new people.
items.note: Describes someone energised by social interaction; extrovert is a related noun.

items.example: He is introverted but contributes thoughtful ideas.
items.note: Often prefers smaller groups or quieter time; not the same as shy.

items.example: She dislikes being the focus of attention at parties.
items.note: Focus of attention is what others are concentrating on.

items.example: Everyone felt tense before the announcement.
items.note: Not relaxed, often because of pressure or anxiety.

items.example: I get wound up when plans change at the last minute.
items.note: Informal: emotionally tense or annoyed; wound is pronounced /waʊnd/ here.

items.example: After the deadline, the whole team felt stressed out.
items.note: Informal description of high stress; stronger than simply busy.

items.example: He seemed relaxed throughout the interview.
items.note: Calm rather than tense; can describe mood or manner.

items.example: Wearing comfortable shoes was a sensible choice.
items.note: Sensible means practical and showing good judgement, not sensitive.

items.example: Her practical advice helped us solve the problem.
items.note: Focuses on realistic actions, not only theories or feelings.

items.example: Our professor is down-to-earth despite her achievements.
items.note: Informal positive phrase for practical, realistic and unpretentious people.

items.example: He is sensitive to criticism but listens carefully.
items.note: Emotionally affected or perceptive; do not confuse with sensible, meaning prudent.

items.example: She got worked up about the unfair accusation.
items.note: Informal phrase for becoming upset, anxious or angry; often get worked up about something.

items.example: He's sociable and makes friends wherever he goes.
items.note: Enjoys social contact; opposite of unsociable.

items.example: The gregarious host greeted every guest personally.
items.note: Often a more formal or written alternative to sociable.

items.example: The quarrelsome neighbours argued over minor issues.
items.note: Frequently starts or becomes involved in arguments.

items.example: He becomes argumentative when he feels ignored.
items.note: Inclined to disagree or argue, not simply able to make an argument.

items.example: It was cruel to mock her in public.
items.note: Causes or enjoys the suffering of others; the opposite of kind-hearted.

items.pt: sádico; que sente prazer no sofrimento alheio
items.example: The film portrays a sadistic villain.
items.note: Strong adjective for taking pleasure in another person's pain.

items.example: Our new supervisor is easy-going about minor mistakes.
items.note: Calm and accepting; not easily upset or rigid.

items.example: The even-tempered coach stayed calm after the defeat.
items.note: Rarely loses their temper, even under stress.

items.example: Her laid-back approach helps everyone feel comfortable.
items.note: Informal, common in spoken English; can sometimes imply too little urgency.

items.example: It is impolite to interrupt someone repeatedly.
items.note: Broad opposite of polite.

items.example: He apologised for his rude response.
items.note: Direct, potentially stronger negative judgement than impolite.

items.example: The ill-mannered guest interrupted the speaker.
items.note: Describes a habitual lack of polite behaviour.

items.example: The company apologised for the discourteous reply.
items.note: Formal or written alternative to impolite.

items.example: I appreciate an honest answer, even when it is difficult.
items.note: Tells the truth; not exactly the same as reliable, which concerns dependability.

items.example: We need a trustworthy person to manage the records.
items.note: Someone you can trust not to deceive or betray you.

items.pt: confiável; pontual; em quem se pode contar
items.example: She is reliable and always arrives when she says she will.
items.note: Consistently does what is expected or promised.

items.example: His apology sounded sincere.
items.note: Expresses genuine feelings or intentions; sincerity is not identical to general honesty.

items.example: He felt jealous when his friend received the award.
items.note: Can mean envious of success or anxious about losing a relationship.

items.example: I was envious of her opportunity to travel.
items.note: Wanting something another person has; unlike jealous, not normally about romantic possessiveness.

items.example: She is determined to finish the course.
items.note: Positive focus on persistence; often determined to do something.

items.example: He remained obstinate despite the new evidence.
items.note: Usually disapproving: refusing to change an opinion when it would be sensible.

items.example: The stubborn manager would not reconsider the decision.
items.note: Usually negative, though determination can be admired in other contexts.

items.example: It was pig-headed to refuse every compromise.
items.note: Informal and strongly disapproving.

items.example: Her thrifty habits helped her save for a house.
items.note: Positive view of spending carefully; contrast stingy.

items.pt: econômico; que faz bom uso de recursos
items.example: The economical driver uses very little fuel.
items.note: Using money or resources efficiently; not identical to economic.

items.example: His friends considered him stingy because he never contributed.
items.note: Negative: unwilling to spend or give money, even when appropriate.

items.example: He is so mean with money that he never offers to pay for coffee.
items.note: In British English, mean can mean stingy; also unkind, or signify in other contexts.

items.example: The tight-fisted landlord refused to replace the heater.
items.note: Informal and disapproving description of unwillingness to spend.

items.example: The miserly owner would not buy new chairs.
items.note: Usually written or formal; strongly negative for excessive reluctance to spend.

items.example: She sounded self-assured during the presentation.
items.note: Positive or neutral: confident in one's abilities.

items.example: The team is confident about its progress.
items.note: Feeling sure or capable; may describe a person or confidence about an outcome.

items.example: His self-important manner annoyed the others.
items.note: Negative: behaving as though you matter more than everyone else.

items.example: The new director came across as arrogant.
items.note: Negatively overconfident or dismissive of others.

items.example: He sounded full of himself after the interview.
items.note: Informal disapproving expression for excessive self-importance.

items.example: Her unconventional solution surprised the committee.
items.note: Does not follow established habits or social conventions; often approving.

items.example: He proposed an original approach to the problem.
items.note: Emphasises novelty and creativity; often positive.

items.example: The artist is known for her eccentric clothes.
items.note: Unusual or unconventional in ways others may find strange or interesting.

items.example: I found his sudden reaction a little odd.
items.note: Informal for unusual; can be mildly negative.

items.example: She has a peculiar habit of collecting old receipts.
items.note: Something distinctive or strange; often implies mild disapproval or curiosity.

items.example: That was a weird question to ask at dinner.
items.note: Common in informal speech; often stronger than odd.

items.example: To be frank, the schedule seems unrealistic.
items.note: Usually approving for direct, honest expression; may feel rude if too abrupt.

items.example: Her direct feedback helped us improve the design.
items.note: Says something clearly and without unnecessary indirectness.

items.example: He was open about the mistakes he had made.
items.note: Can mean willing to communicate frankly, as well as accessible or not closed.

items.example: His blunt criticism upset several colleagues.
items.note: Often negative: very direct without considering other people's feelings.

items.example: She was taken aback by his abrupt reply.
items.note: Short or sudden in a manner that may seem rude; also used of sudden changes.

items.example: The brusque receptionist barely greeted us.
items.note: Strongly suggests an unfriendly, abrupt manner; relatively formal.

items.example: He gave a curt answer and returned to work.
items.note: Brief to the point of seeming impolite; contrasts with frank or direct.

items.example: Her broad-minded approach welcomes different opinions.
items.note: Positive: willing to consider ideas and lifestyles unlike one's own.

items.example: The campaign was criticised for its unprincipled tactics.
items.note: Negative: lacking moral principles; not a precise synonym for broad-minded.

items.example: Some parents prefer a more permissive approach.
items.note: Allows considerable freedom; judgement depends on context.

items.example: An enquiring student wants to understand how things work.
items.note: British spelling; usually approving for curious and questioning.

items.pt: curioso; cheio de perguntas; intrometido em certos contextos
items.example: The inquisitive journalist asked a series of detailed questions.
items.note: Often curious in a positive way but may imply prying; compare nosy.

items.example: She thought it was nosy to ask about his salary.
items.note: Informal, clearly negative for excessive curiosity about other people's private lives.

items.example: Her generous donation supported the local library.
items.note: Willing to give or share; contrast extravagant and stingy.

items.example: They criticised his extravagant spending habits.
items.note: Can imply excessive or wasteful spending rather than healthy generosity.

items.example: She was innocent of any wrongdoing.
items.note: Free from guilt; may also suggest lack of experience or malice.

items.example: It was naive to trust an unknown website immediately.
items.note: Often disapproving of excessive trust or lack of worldly experience.

items.example: He is ambitious and hopes to lead a research group.
items.note: Usually approving or neutral for strong goals, unlike pushy.

items.pt: insistente demais; forçado; que se impõe (informal)
items.example: The pushy salesperson would not take no for an answer.
items.note: Informal, negative: advances one's aims too aggressively.

items.example: She was assertive without raising her voice.
items.note: Positive: expresses needs and opinions confidently while respecting others.

items.example: His aggressive tone discouraged discussion.
items.note: When about interpersonal behaviour, often negative; can also mean forceful in sport or business.

items.example: The others resented his bossy instructions.
items.note: Informal disapproval of ordering others around unnecessarily.

items.section: D · Understanding the connotation of a trait
items.example: The adjective stubborn has a more negative connotation than determined.
items.note: The favourable or unfavourable associations a word carries beyond its basic meaning.

items.word: one person's meat is another person's poison
items.pt: o que agrada a um pode desagradar a outro
items.section: D · Understanding the connotation of a trait
items.example: We disagreed about the music, but one person's meat is another person's poison.
items.note: Proverb-like expression meaning that tastes and judgements differ from person to person.

items.example: She is quiet, but not necessarily unsociable.
items.note: Does not enjoy or seek company; not automatically the same as being introverted.

items.example: The receptionist was courteous to every visitor.
items.note: Polite and respectful; opposite of rude and close to polite.

items.example: A kind-hearted neighbour offered to help.
items.note: Shows kindness and sympathy; contrasts with cruel.

sectionsChecked: D: One person’s meat is another person’s poison (connotations and register)
